query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A single-step phase-selective intermediate-temperature annealing following cold or cryogenic rolling will reduce dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries and enhance ductility without sacrificing, and potentially even improving, the alloy’s high strength.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase (fcc + B2) lamellar microstructure that exhibits limited tensile ductility at room temperature due to dislocation pile-ups near phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a moderate-temperature (approximately 650–750 °C) short-duration annealing treatment after cold or cryogenic rolling to induce partial recrystallization of the soft fcc lamellae, while preserving the finer B2 regions.
generation.conditions: Perform rolling to a significant thickness reduction (e.g., ~8–40%) at or below room temperature, followed by holding at the selected intermediate annealing temperature for about 30–60 minutes. Conduct subsequent uniaxial tensile tests at room temperature to evaluate mechanical properties.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized recrystallization in the fcc phase disrupts dislocation pile-ups and mitigates stress concentrations at the lamellar interfaces, while retaining the finer B2 structure.
generation.mechanism: Newly formed recrystallized grains within the ductile phase accommodate strain more uniformly, preventing microcracking and catastrophic failure at interfaces. The untransformed B2 phase provides sufficient barrier strength and maintains high overall load-bearing capacity.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, the partially recrystallized eutectic alloy will achieve up to ~25% or greater elongation to failure while retaining or surpassing the baseline yield strength of ~1–1.2 GPa, potentially reaching 1.2–2.0 GPa under optimized conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated as-cast material generally shows ductility near 10–15% with yield strengths of ~1–1.2 GPa under room-temperature tension.
generation.boundary: Excessively high annealing temperatures or extended annealing times can coarsen the B2 lamellae or lead to over-recrystallization, eroding strength gains. The optimal time-temperature combination requires empirical calibration for each specific alloy composition and initial rolling strain.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature and duration for phase-selective recrystallization will vary with alloy composition and rolling reduction and requires experimental fine-tuning. Some samples may experience over-recrystallization and lose strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare comparable sets of samples with identical cold or cryogenic rolling reductions, then anneal them at systematically varied temperatures (e.g., 600 °C, 650 °C, 700 °C, and 750 °C) and times (e.g., 15, 30, 60, 120 minutes). Conduct standard tensile tests to determine if the proposed treatment yields reproducible increases in ductility while maintaining or enhancing strength. Compare as-cast, rolled-only, and over-annealed conditions as controls.
measurements: Microstructural characterization via SEM/TEM to quantify recrystallized fraction and lamellar refinement
Room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, strain hardening rate, and total elongation
Fractography to check for the presence or absence of microcracks at lamellar boundaries
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples show no improvement in ductility or if significant coarsening of B2 lamella occurs at intermediate temperatures, invalidating the predicted mechanical gains and microstructure evolution, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. The present study for the first time demonstrated that cryo-deformation and annealing could be a novel microstructural design strategy for overcoming strength-ductility trade off in multiphase high ent

Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys showed that a fine fcc/B2 lamellar microstructure can offer balanced strength and ductility. Subsequent studies refined these lamellae through cryo-rolling, warm rolling, and targeted annealing, achieving improved strength-ductility responses via hierarchical microstructure formation and partial phase recrystallization. Despite these gains, the key challenge remains mitigating boundary-related crack initiation and optimizing dislocation interactions to further raise ductility while preserving or boosting strength.
decision.unsolved: Existing thermo-mechanical methods reduce but do not fully eliminate dislocation pile-ups and stress concentrations at phase boundaries, which still limit ductility and lead to catastrophic brittle failure. A single-step procedure capable of locally refining or adjusting boundary structure is needed to address these issues without resorting to multiple complex processing steps or compositional modifications.
decision.lever: A phase-selective intermediate-temperature annealing after cold or cryogenic rolling to induce partial recrystallization of the soft phase while retaining fine B2 lamellae
decision.why: Partial recrystallization within the more ductile phase disrupts dislocation pile-ups at the soft/hard phase interfaces, reducing boundary stress concentrations and microcracking. This strategy retains the finely spaced B2 lamellae for high strength while providing newly recrystallized, strain-accommodating regions in the ductile phase that improve overall fracture resistance. Prior work on phase-selective recrystallization in EHEAs has shown dramatic ductility gains with little or no strength penalty, and this approach directly targets the local boundary issues that drive brittleness. Mechanical tests should employ standard room-temperature uniaxial tension to evaluate enhanced ductility (e.g., >25% elongation to failure) and maintained or improved yield strength (e.g., 1.2–2 GPa). A falsification test would involve using an annealing temperature or schedule that does not achieve phase-selective recrystallization (e.g., too low or too high temperature), to confirm that the improved ductility does not manifest when the boundary structures remain unreformed or are coarsened excessively.
